displayQuote: The perfect is the enemy of the good

meta.title: Who really said "The perfect is the enemy of the good"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Voltaire really did publish it — as verse in La Bégueule (1772) — but he credited an older Italian proverb, and the literal sense is “the best,” not “the perfect.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The perfect is the enemy of the good'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, it's Voltaire — La Bégueule, 1772. But he credited an Italian proverb, and “le mieux” means “the best,” not “the perfect.”

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Voltaire wrote “le mieux est l’ennemi du bien” in the opening couplet of his verse tale ‘La Bégueule’ (1772) and used the same maxim in ‘Questions sur l’Encyclopédie’ (1770) — though in both places he credited “un sage Italien.” The familiar English is a translation of that line (more literally, “the best is the enemy of the good”).

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: La Bégueule, conte moral (in Contes en vers)

source.excerpt:
Dans ses écrits un sage Italien
Dit que le mieux est l’ennemi du bien.
(In his writings a wise Italian / says that the best is the enemy of the good.)
trail: The maxim appears verbatim in Voltaire’s verse tale — “Dit que le mieux est l’ennemi du bien” — in the La Bégueule text on Wikisource ↗.

Wikiquote ↗ dates the line to La Bégueule (1772), notes Voltaire ascribed it to an unnamed “Italian sage,” and traces it to the proverb ‘Il meglio è nemico del bene,’ documented in Orlando Pescetti’s work in 1603.

Wikipedia ↗ records that Voltaire quoted the Italian proverb in the 1770 Questions sur l’Encyclopédie and that a close variant, “Le mieux est le mortel ennemi du bien,” appears in Montesquieu’s Pensées (c. 1726).
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular English keeps the maxim but drops Voltaire’s own credit to “a wise Italian”
source.excerptNote: Voltaire opens the poem by quoting the maxim, then spends the tale illustrating it — a restless woman who cannot leave well enough alone. Note “le mieux” means “the best/the better,” which the English rendered as “the perfect.”

sourceLink.text: La Bégueule, full text on Wikisource

source.rightsNote: The quote is public domain: Voltaire’s text was published in 1772 and he died in 1778. Modern English translations of the line carry no separate claim on the maxim itself.

author.name: Voltaire
author.heading: About Voltaire
author.bio: Voltaire (pen name of François-Marie Arouet) was a leading figure of the French Enlightenment, famous for his wit, his advocacy of civil liberties, and works such as ‘Candide’ and the ‘Dictionnaire philosophique.’ He was a prolific aphorist who often reworked older sayings — and, characteristically, he introduced this one by crediting “a wise Italian” rather than claiming it as his own.

cite.sourceCitation: Voltaire. “La Bégueule, conte moral.” In Contes en vers. Paris, 1772. Opening lines: “Dans ses écrits un sage Italien / Dit que le mieux est l’ennemi du bien.”

misattribution.heading: The record, straightened
misattribution.intro: The credit to Voltaire is essentially right — but two things are widely misremembered about it.

items.why: Voltaire did not coin the maxim; he explicitly quoted “un sage Italien.” It descends from the Italian proverb ‘Il meglio è nemico del bene,’ documented in Orlando Pescetti’s collection in 1603, per Wikiquote ↗, and earlier French forms circulated before 1772 — the Wiktionnaire ↗ cites a 1745 Mercure de France version and a 1757 writer calling it “ce vieux proverbe.”

items.who: “the perfect is the enemy of the good”
items.why: Voltaire’s word is “le mieux” — ‘the best’ or ‘the better,’ not ‘the perfect.’ The literal sense recorded on Wikipedia ↗ is “the best is the enemy of the good.”

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: Voltaire really did publish the line — in La Bégueule, 1772 ↗ — but as his rendering of an older Italian proverb, and its literal meaning is “the best is the enemy of the good.”

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: The maxim endures because it names a real trap: the pursuit of an ideal outcome can prevent a perfectly workable one. Voltaire deployed it as a moral about restlessness — his heroine cannot leave a good life alone — and the line has since become a staple of engineering, medicine, economics, and management, usually as a caution against over-optimizing.

Its journey is itself an example of the idea: a compact old proverb, ‘good enough’ as it was, outlived every attempt to improve on it — and it reached the English-speaking world through a slightly imperfect translation that stuck.
